methodology.record_unit: Distinct source profile/food-use cluster, medicinal indication/dose, procedure or named inventory entry; repeated contexts retained. No preliminary numerical target.

classifications.verified_guidance: Limited supported safety or permission principle; no field specimen, complete identification key or medical treatment is certified.
classifications.source_derived_reference: Faithful source reference; whole detail not independently validated.
classifications.needs_review: Consequential unsupported, incomplete, unsafe or contradicted detail requiring resolution.

limitations: All 54 PDF pages were text-reviewed, except that the cover has no substantive extractable text and was visually reviewed. Twenty-one selected source pages received visual inspection; four were also inspected at larger size. This is not a botanical authentication of every photograph or a visual audit of every map.

The cover has no printed number. Printed 2-26 equals PDF 2-26; PDF 27-54 equals printed 24-51. Printed labels 24, 25 and 26 therefore occur twice. The running title changes at PDF 27, and the contents is stale for several section locations. PDF positions are indispensable citation disambiguators.

The source uses unnumbered main headings. CH01-CH08 are editorial review sections, not invented source chapter numbers. Kudzu ends and clover begins on PDF 17, so sections CH02 and CH03 share that boundary page; the ledger assigns it to CH03 while retaining all citations.

Each named list entry, profile identification, coherent food-use cluster, named recipe/process and distinct medicinal indication or dosing row is a record. A cluster of several synonyms or related indications can count once. Profile food-use clusters preserve multiple culinary suggestions together. Counts are actual extraction units, not unique species, approved tasks or a forced target.

There are 21 main profiles, 25 additional greens entries, 9 berry entries, 3 root entries and 11 tree entries. Repeated names are retained for source traceability; the lists are not validated shopping or eating lists. Medical assertions are faithful paraphrases and not treatment instructions.

No plant specimen was examined, no local harvest site was visited and no meal, extract, mushroom or medicinal dose was tested. No complete field-identification key or herbal treatment is verified. Virginia law and seasonal context were checked; exact local occurrence, parcel access and collection permission remain unknown.

Specific high-consequence claims were independently checked against primary government and Extension sources. Many other medicinal bullets were screened and held for missing clinical support rather than individually exhaustively literature-reviewed. Needs review does not always mean disproven; source-derived reference does not mean safe.

Evidence was accessed October 31, 2026; no immutable website snapshots were archived. W01 and W05 are two scopes on the same FDA page, not independent corroboration. Failed DCR/DOF/WMA page opens were not counted as reviewed evidence; Virginia park law was checked directly in the official Administrative Code.

Editorial milestones and topic names do not map to existing app IDs or demonstrate calories, water, dietary adequacy or household progress. All execution remains held. The root-cellar book is deferred at the user’s request; limited storage mentions within this book are still documented.
Schema v1.2.0 is reused without modification. Earlier finalized books remain unchanged. No HomePrep/LPI app code, import, deployment, purchase or external message was performed.

record.title: Investigation of Illnesses: Morel Mushrooms (May 2023)
record.finding: Qualified expert identification is important. This source directly addresses mushrooms, not every plant; applying caution to plant shortcuts is reviewer risk analysis.

record.title: Storing Up for Winter with Forageables
record.finding: The official Virginia article supports positive identification, minimizing damage and obtaining permission. It also discusses seasonal food and acorn leaching; its older WMA-law summary is not treated as a current permit.

record.publisher: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
record.title: Dandelion
record.finding: No compelling scientific evidence supports dandelion for a health condition. Food use and medicinal dosing differ; interactions and safety uncertainty remain.

record.publisher: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
record.title: Red Clover
record.finding: Menopause and bone-density results are inconsistent; supplement safety in pregnancy/breastfeeding is a concern. This is not evidence about every Trifolium species.

record.title: Morel and other wild-mushroom recommendations
record.finding: Cooking cannot guarantee safety; false-morel toxins may remain after heating. Expert identification and appropriate storage are necessary. Same page as W01, a separately scoped evidence locator, not an independent source.

record.title: Preventing Rat Lungworm
record.finding: Do not eat raw or undercooked snails/slugs in affected areas. Wash raw vegetables thoroughly. This does not certify purging, an insect recipe or Virginia prevalence.

record.title: Venomous Snakes at Work
record.finding: Prompt medical care is needed; do not use folk therapies. Plantain poultice/juice is not supported as snakebite treatment.

record.title: 4VAC5-30-50. Flowers, plants, minerals, etc.
record.locator: Current rule text, including personal edible-collection exception
record.finding: The rule generally protects vegetation but expressly permits personal or individual gathering of edible fruits, berries, fungi and nuts. This does not authorize digging roots, stripping bark or tapping; site scope still matters.

record.title: Plantago major
record.finding: The profile describes flowering stems under twelve inches, contradicting the book's seven-to-twenty-foot description. The source does not validate medicinal uses or identify a specimen.

record.title: Prunus virginiana
record.finding: Stems, leaves and seeds have cyanogenic hazards. The book's human-use bark claims cannot be treated as safe doses or the warning restricted to livestock.

record.title: Cassava and bamboo shoots
record.finding: Only selected bamboo species are used as food; cyanogenic shoots require appropriate preparation and discarded cooking water. Commercial canned-product reassurance does not validate arbitrary home canning.

record.title: Homemade maple syrup
record.locator: Tapping, sap yield and evaporation instructions
record.finding: Proper taps and food-grade collection are described. Syrup concentrates sap by evaporation to a controlled endpoint; adding thirty-five parts water is not this process.

record.title: Salicis cortex
record.finding: Defined willow-bark preparations have restrictions, salicylate interactions and gastrointestinal adverse effects; childbirth leaf chewing is not validated by this monograph.

record.title: Healthy Gardening Practices to Reduce Exposure to Lead-Contaminated Soil
record.locator: Soil testing, siting and produce preparation
record.finding: Assess actual contamination and avoid sources; soil testing and exposure controls matter. This is not evidence for a universal one-hundred-foot boundary or uphill safety.

record.title: Food Allergies: What You Need to Know
record.finding: Food allergy can be serious; a mild reaction does not establish a mild allergy. A taste is not an identification or allergy-clearance procedure.

record.title: Complementary and Alternative Medicine
record.finding: No food or herb combination is proven to slow, cure or prevent recurrence of cancer. Clinical care must not be replaced with this book's cancer claims.

record.publisher: NIH National Library of Medicine / MedlinePlus
record.title: Poisoning first aid
record.finding: Do not wait for symptoms in suspected poisoning; seek poison-control or emergency guidance. This is not support for a daylily antidote or other herbal treatment.

record.title: What You Should Know about Eye Drops
record.finding: Drugs used in eyes must be sterile. A homemade rose infusion is not an established sterile treatment for eye infection.

record.publisher: National Center for Home Food Preservation
record.title: How Do I Preserve Foods?
record.finding: Food preservation needs food- and process-specific instructions; broad drying, fermentation or oil-extraction statements are not complete validated methods.

record.title: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms
record.locator: Key points, heavy bleeding after pregnancy, chest/heart warning signs
record.finding: Heavy postpartum bleeding and listed serious maternal symptoms warrant immediate medical care, rather than an unvalidated pollen or willow preparation.

record.title: Identification must establish the actual specimen
record.guidance: Common names, resemblance, an app, odor, a single feature, a photograph or confidence do not establish a safe meal. Learn complete local identification and toxic lookalikes with qualified help; reject uncertain specimens. Assess exact species, plant part, maturity and preparation. A small taste cannot clear unknown plants or demonstrate absence of allergy. None of this examination’s plant profiles is an approved field identification key.

record.title: No universal clean-site shortcut
record.guidance: Assess land use, treatment history, contamination and water/soil conditions. Uphill position, neglected growth, washing and a 100-foot road setback do not demonstrate toxin-free plants. EPA’s lead guidance concerns actual testing and exposure controls, not certification of every roadside or urban forage site.

record.title: Medicinal claims remain unvalidated
record.guidance: Food use, traditional use and laboratory activity are not proof of clinical efficacy or a safe medicinal dose. NCCIH finds no compelling dandelion efficacy evidence and inconsistent red-clover findings for several promoted uses. NCI does not support these foods/herbs as cancer treatment. Other specific herbal claims here were screened for gaps, not each exhaustively searched in clinical literature. Do not replace appropriate medical care with them; clinician review must address diagnosis, interactions, dose, age and pregnancy. No pediatric wine, wound poultice, botanical antibiotic or oral treatment has been approved by this examination.

record.title: Poisoning, bleeding and eye-treatment claims require proper care
record.guidance: Daylily juice is not an established arsenic antidote. In suspected poisoning, seek poison-control or emergency help without waiting for symptoms; do not use a homemade antidote. Internal bleeding, postpartum hemorrhage and serious cardiac symptoms need urgent clinical evaluation rather than herbal dosing. CDC identifies heavy postpartum bleeding and serious maternal heart symptoms as urgent warning signs. Homemade rose tea is not a sterile eye medicine; FDA requires ophthalmic medicines to be sterile. These constraints address particular claims; the reviewer does not claim to have validated every medical condition in this book.

record.title: Plantain does not replace snakebite care
record.guidance: Get medical help immediately for suspected venomous snakebite. CDC advises against folk therapies and attempts to remove venom. Reject plantain poultices and juice as an antidote; do not delay care to gather or prepare herbs.

record.title: Cyanogenic plants and unassessed plant parts
record.guidance: Chokecherry stems, leaves and seeds have cyanogenic hazards; the book’s bark remedies and incomplete human warning must remain held. The stated many-small-seeds description also needs botanical reconciliation rather than serving as a key. Bamboo needs species-appropriate preparation, including discarding cooking water under the cited FSANZ guidance. Its reassurance about commercial canned shoots does not endorse arbitrary home canning or raw shoot juice. Serviceberry seed tea and other nonfruit medicinal uses remain unassessed; no universal safe part or dose is inferred.

record.title: Mushroom shortcuts and cooking guarantees fail
record.guidance: Require expert identification of each mushroom; a hollow interior, white flesh, cap color, lack of gills or cooking alone cannot certify safety. FDA reports illness associated with true morels and says cooking cannot guarantee safety. False-morel toxins can persist after cooking. No mushroom entry in this book is promoted to a validated consumption protocol.

record.title: Correct scale, illustration and range errors
record.guidance: Plantain flowering stems are not seven to twenty feet tall; the consulted Extension description says under twelve inches. The Typha figure visibly labels Carex typhina, a different plant, and is unsuitable as its range map. The burdock map URL and common-name scope require reconciliation with the Arctium lappa heading. The canna page contains stray layout letters. Range shading, broad ornamental distributions and this book’s incomplete keys do not demonstrate wild food availability in Virginia. Original details remain preserved rather than silently repaired.

record.title: Preparation and storage need complete methods
record.guidance: Use food-specific validated handling, detoxification, cooking, drying, fermentation and storage instructions. The acorn schedules, below-70-F wet holding, two-year storage, three-month tigernut drying and blanket herb-oil/fermentation advice are not validated processes. Bitterness, floating, sprouting, firmness or a calendar duration are not general safety tests. Cattail gluten/allergen claims and cooking-as-a-guarantee against tuber gas are unsupported. No replacement recipe or cellar construction is supplied.

record.title: Wild invertebrates are not automatically food
record.guidance: Identify an appropriate edible species, assess contamination and allergy, and use a validated food-specific preparation. Broad references to grubs, beetles, worms and ants are insufficient. Snail purging does not establish pathogen elimination; CDC warns against raw/undercooked snails and slugs in affected areas. That warning does not establish Virginia prevalence or a universal cooking schedule.

record.title: Maple syrup concentrates sap
record.guidance: Reject the instruction to add thirty-five parts water to one part sap. Extension describes evaporating water from collected sap to a controlled syrup endpoint. Tree and season affect yields; use tree-safe tapping and suitable food-contact equipment. A V-shaped wound, makeshift can-lid spile and thickness-by-eye are not the cited complete method. Sap-to-syrup yield ratios are not added-water recipes.

record.title: Willow is not risk-free aspirin
record.guidance: Defined willow-bark preparations have salicylate-related restrictions, interactions and gastrointestinal adverse effects. EMA excludes children/adolescents and third-trimester pregnancy for the assessed medicines. This does not validate chewing Salix alba leaves during childbirth or its use as a universal safe food. Do not substitute wild bark/leaves for a standardized medicine.

record.title: Virginia access differs by land manager
record.guidance: Get landowner permission and check current site-specific collection rules. The current Virginia park rule permits personal or individual collection of edible fruits, berries, fungi and nuts, while otherwise prohibiting taking or damaging vegetation except authorized scientific collecting. This exception does not authorize uprooting plants, stripping bark or tapping trees. The DCR search excerpt omitted this exception; this examination uses the actual Administrative Code text. DWR’s older WMA summary is context, not a current property authorization. Verify the exact land manager, activity and any site restrictions.
